title: Start-up Visa vs High Impact Start-up Pilot: Field by Field
excerpt: The old programme has published rules. The pilot has published a name. Here is the comparison, with the blanks left blank.
keyTakeaway: Of the fields that define the Start-up Visa, capital minimums, language level and the designated-organization model, none has been published for the pilot yet.
summaryEn: A field-by-field comparison of the paused Start-up Visa and the announced High Impact Start-up Pilot, showing what IRCC has and has not published.

faq.q: What did the Start-up Visa require?
faq.a: A commitment from a designated organization (CAD 200,000 from a venture fund or CAD 75,000 from an angel group), CLB 5 in all four skills and a qualifying business. The pilot's requirements are unpublished.

content:
People ask whether the new pilot "keeps" the old rules. The only defensible answer is a table where one column is full and the other is mostly empty. The old column below is from IRCC's own manual for assessing Start-up Business Class applications. The pilot column is whatever IRCC has said, which is very little. Checked 5 November 2026.

FieldStart-up Visa (paused)High Impact Start-up Pilot
StatusPaused since 30 June 2026Announced, not open
Who backs the founderA designated organization: venture fund, angel group or incubatorNot published
Minimum committed capitalCAD 200,000 from a venture fund, CAD 75,000 from an angel groupNot published
LanguageCLB 5 in all four skills, test under two years oldNot published
OwnershipEach applicant at least 10% of voting rights; applicants and the designated entity together more than 50%Not published
Target applicantFounders with a qualifying business and a commitment"Elite entrepreneurs" (Departmental Plan, as reported)
IntakeA limit of 10 complete group applications per designated organization per year since 1 April 2024Not published

Sources: IRCC, assessing the application; IRCC transition binder; immigration.ca for the Departmental Plan wording.

How to read the empty cells

An empty cell is not a hint. It is not "probably the same" or "probably tougher". Trade press expects a more selective pilot, with closer checks on the business and on designated organizations, but that is the author's inference from IRCC's wording, not IRCC's text.

What the comparison is good for

It tells you which parts of your preparation are safe to start now. Clean ownership, evidence of traction and a language result that will not expire matter under the old rules and will almost certainly matter under any new ones. It does not tell you what the pilot will ask for, because nobody can yet.

What each column's source can and cannot tell you

The old column comes from a manual written for officers assessing real applications, so it is precise: capital minimums, ownership thresholds, a language level. The pilot column comes from planning documents, so it is general: a name, a target group, a direction. Comparing a precise document with a general one will always make the pilot look like it is "missing" things. It is not missing them. They have not been written yet.

A caution about "faster"

Some commentary suggests the pilot may process stronger candidates faster. IRCC has not said so, and the old programme published no processing time either, so "faster than what?" has no answer. We do not put any processing figure in the table for that reason.

What to watch for

When IRCC publishes the pilot's rules, the first things to compare are the same ones in this table: who backs the founder, what capital that backer must commit, what language level applies, and how many places exist. If any of those arrive, a blank in the table becomes a filled cell, with its source.

The same table, with sources linked per cell and a filter for the blanks, is on our pilot page.
